blocks.text: I note this because the hitherto unidentified Hebrew תחמס thachmas corresponds exactly to the Arabic name ظليم [ẓalīm] dtalim. For as ظليم [ẓalīm] dtalim comes from ظلم [ẓalama] dtalima, which means to be unjust and to oppress, so תחמס thachmas comes from the verb חמס chamas, which has the same meaning as the Arabic ظلم [ẓalama] dtalima. Accordingly, in the Pentateuch, nearly every time חמס occurs in the sacred text, ظلم [ẓulm] occurs in the Arabic paraphrasts. Thus in Gen. VI, 11. the Hebrew reads: The earth was full of חמס, iniquity; the Erpenianus has بالظلم [bi-l-ẓulm]. So too in verse 13, where the other Arabic version, published in Paris, also has تملات ظلما [tamallaʾat ẓulman]. And in chapter 16, verse 5, where the Hebrew has חמסי עליך, My wrong be upon you, that is, the wrong done to me will fall back upon you, both Arabic versions have ظلمي عليك [ẓulmī ʿalayka]. And in Gen. XLIX, 5., for the Hebrew כלי חמס, instruments of iniquity, both render آلة الظلم [ālat al-ẓulm]. Likewise in Exod. XXIII, 1. and Deut. XIX, 16., עד חמס, a witness of iniquity, is in both شاهد ظلم [shāhid ẓulm]. Examples of this kind may also be seen in the other books of Scripture. Thus Psal. VII, 17. Let his iniquity come down upon his own pate. Hebrew חמסו, Arabic ظلمه [ẓulmuhu]. Psal. XI, 5. He who loves iniquity. Hebrew חמס, Arabic الظلم [al-ẓulm]. Psal. XXV, 19. They hate me שנאת חמס, with a hatred of iniquity: Arabic ظلما [ẓulman], unjustly. See also Psal. XXVII, 12. and LVIII, 2. and LXXII, 14. and LXXIII, 6. and CXL, 2. 5. 12. So also in the Prophets. Thus Esa. LX, 18. There shall no more be heard חמס, iniquity in your land: Arabic ظلم [ẓulm]. Ezech. XLV, 9. Remove חמס, iniquity: Arabic الظلم [al-ẓulm]. Amos III, 10. Who store up חמס, iniquity: Arabic ظلما [ẓulman]. Ion. III, 8. Let everyone turn from his evil way, ומן החמס, and from the iniquity that is in his hands: Arabic ومن الظلم [wa-min al-ẓulm]. Hab. I, 2. I cry out to you חמס, suffering oppression (that is, violence), as Jerome has it: Arabic مظلوم [maẓlūm], oppressed. Since, then, the Arabic ظلم [ẓulm] is exactly the same as the Hebrew חמס, [col. 235] [II, 834] as so many examples have shown, a highly probable conjecture follows: that ظليم [ẓalīm] is also the same as תחמס, and תחמס the same as ظليم [ẓalīm]; that is, that both words denote the ostrich, and specifically the male. How probable, and I might almost say necessary, this reasoning is, all who understand the genius of these languages know. It is entirely certain, therefore, that as in Moses בת היענה is the female ostrich, so the next word, התחמס, is the male ostrich. Nor is it anything new for the sexes of animals to be distinguished in this way. Thus Avicenna and Abenbitar, as we have noted, treat نعام [naʿām] naam and ظليم [ẓalīm] dtalim, that is, the female and the male ostrich, in separate chapters. And in Moses himself, Gen. XXXII, 15., we read that Jacob offered Esau she-goats and he-goats, ewes and rams. And in Gen. XLV, 23., Joseph sends his father ten male asses and as many she-asses. But, you will say, why is the sex distinguished in the ostrich rather than in the eagle, the raven, etc.? The reason is ready to hand. Since נשר comprises the whole genus of eagles, and עורב the whole genus of ravens, it was enough for Moses to prohibit נשר and עורב. But the Hebrews have no generic name for the ostrich. For תחמס denotes only the males, and בת יענה only the females, as does רננים in Job. Therefore, lest by prohibiting one of these he should seem to permit the other, he had to prohibit both expressly ^{(2)}.
